Rules / Modernization

SK1082 Use the indexer

list.ElementAt(i) is list[i]: the language has syntax for the operation the LINQ extension is standing in for.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

ElementAt exists so that a bare IEnumerable<T> can be indexed at all — it walks the sequence when it has to and reaches for IList<T> when it can. On a List<T> the second branch is the only one that ever runs, so the call is a generic entry point wrapped around the indexer the receiver already declares. The indexer is shorter, needs no using System.Linq, and says the collection has positions rather than find me the element in that position, which is the distinction that matters when the next reader asks whether the receiver is a sequence or a list.

Example

Instead of:

var first = entries.ElementAt(0);
var chosen = entries.ElementAt(index);

Write:

var first = entries[0];
var chosen = entries[index];

When it does not fire

⚠ The receiver is `List<T>` or `ImmutableList<T>` and nothing else, and the reason is the exception the rewrite would otherwise change. Enumerable.ElementAt bounds-checks itself and throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException on every path; List<T> and ImmutableList<T> throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException from their indexers, so on those two the type, and not merely the fact, of the failure survives the rewrite. An array does not qualify and is the shape this exclusion exists for: array.ElementAt(i) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException and array[i] throws IndexOutOfRangeException, so a catch written for one stops catching. IList<T> and IReadOnlyList<T> are excluded because an array is a legal value for both, which puts the exception type back out of reach. ⚠ `ImmutableArray<T>` is refused a guard earlier than that, and the difference was found by a sabotage that turned nothing red: System.Linq.ImmutableArrayExtensions declares its own ElementAt(this ImmutableArray<T>, int), so the call never binds to Enumerable.ElementAt and the receiver set is never consulted for it — adding it to that set changes nothing at all. The negative fixture that actually holds the receiver set down is Collection<T>, which binds Enumerable.ElementAt, declares an int indexer, and is refused by the closed list alone. This is the same receiver set as SK4030, arrived at from the opposite direction — that rule substitutes one method for another and this one removes the call in favour of language syntax. ⚠ ElementAtOrDefault is not reported: it returns default(T) where the indexer throws, so there is no indexer expression that means the same thing. ⚠ The Index-typed ElementAt(^1) overload is refused, because list[^1] is a different rewrite with a C# 8 floor and is SK1060's subject. ⚠ The call must resolve to System.Linq.Enumerable, must be the extension spelling on a receiver rather than the static one, and must not be a conditional access — xs?.ElementAt(i) becomes xs?[i], which is a different edit. ⚠ UseIndexedProperty's own shape, an explicit get_Item call, is not covered and cannot be: C# rejects a direct accessor call with CS0571, so the inspection has no C# source form to report on and this rule takes the reachable half of the concept.
